newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh PM Hasina seen walking tightrope.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM Hasina seen walking tightrope.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina began her second year in office on Monday with a fresh vow to turn her impoverished country into a "land of gold".

But while her term in office has thus far provided hope of a better future for this impoverished nation, Bangladesh still faces mounting challenges on both the political and economic fronts, officials and analysts said on Monday.
Hasina, the daughter of Bangladesh's independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led her Awami League party to power one year ago Monday, 21 years after her father "Mujib" was killed in an army coup.
She has said her priorities are to improve the lives of Bangladesh's 120 million people through administrative and economic reforms and to alter the nation's blighted image.
Her performance in office has been closely watched by both her allies and foes, as well as by foreign aid donors who pump nearly $2 billion a year into the impoverished South Asian country.

But while saying a full assessment of Hasina could not be made after only 12 months, an Asian diplomat praised her reform plans, especially those intended to speed up privatisation and shore up the banking sector, which faces a severe crisis over bad loans.
Hasina, unlike her predecessors, has kept a cool head in setting her priorities, and has not jumped on any quick-fix measures, analysts said.
"I have drawn up many plans and projects for fulfilling my election pledges. We have to implement them within three years' time," she told senior officials last week.
"We have so many things to do...but time is running out," she said. A European diplomat said: "Hasina made rampant promises apparently to keep the electorate happy until the next election (in 2001).
But some doubt whether Hasina will be able to keep all of her promises.
"The people are waiting for dividends from her pledges. They (dividends) will set the standard (of people's support for her government) and the future course for her," he told Reuters.

Hasina also faces fierce pressure from political opponents, particularly the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) led by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, which has threatened to oust her government.

Hasina signed a 30-year treaty with India last December on sharing the water of the mighty Ganges river, removing the worst irritant in relations between the two countries. She later reached another deal that led to the return of tribal refugees to Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts from exile in the northeast Indian state of Tripura.
But the BNP cites the treaties as evidence that Hasina plans to sell out Bangladesh to its giant neighbor.
"It is high time we oppose the government tooth and nail, and force it from power," Khaleda said last week.

Analysts said Hasina is walking a "tightrope" as she starts the second year of her five-year term in office, but she faced no immediate risk of falling from power because there have been more pluses than minuses in her first year in office, they said.

"Her major political success is that a multi-party democracy and the parliament are still functioning," said Dr. Atiur Rahman, a senior research fellow with the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies.
He said that to sustain political stability, Hasina must endeavour to confine any outright political opposition to within parliament.
The country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew 5.7 percent in the 1996/97 (July-June) financial year and inflation was kept below four percent, which Rahman said was "not bad".
But he also noted that GDP growth was only 0.4 percent higher than in 1995/96 -- which was not enough given that the population grew two percent in 1996/97.

"Hasina's government has to take the growth rate higher than 7 percent (during her tenure), restore health and vigour in the banking sector, spur industrial growth and cut poverty. These are all big challenges," he said. Hasina's personal

initiative helped to placate recent unrest by government employees over pay and other issues, but officials say the issue may resurface as the employees remain sharply divided by political allegiance between the Awami League and BNP.

Analysts noted that Hasina had been trying hard to keep the armed forces happy to prevent a return to military rule. Army generals governed Bangladesh for nearly 15 years after Mujib died, along with most of his family, in the August 1975 coup.
Her government recently joined several regional and other trade groupings trying to improve trade and commerce.
But these could backfire if the nation's people did not get the economic benefits shortly, analysts said.
